events.title: California Traffic Engineering License Exam Review
events.description: DescriptionWe monitor the exam board’s requirements closely. This course will be updated with the latest reference requirements provided by the board as soon as they are released, ensuring all students study from the appropriate standards for the exam. This twelve-session, live, online training course is intended to help practicing transportation professionals prepare for the California Traffic Engineer exam to become a licensed professional Traffic Engineer in California. The course includes a set of sample problems for each session with fully-developed solutions to give examinees more opportunity to hone in their test-taking skills. The twelve sessions are designed to assist test takers on the topics identified on the Traffic Engineer Examination Content Outline on the California Board for Professional Engineers, Land Surveyors, and Geologists website. It provides strategies and techniques needed to manage time and solve exam questions under pressure, and apply required manuals, handbooks, and references, such as the California Manual of Uniform Traffic Control Devices (CA MUTCD), Highway Capacity Manual (HCM), Caltrans Traffic Manual, ITE Trip Generation Handbook and ITE Parking Generation Handbook. Throughout the course, practice exam problems and solutions covering all four main areas of traffic engineering (i.e., planning, operations, studies & analysis, and design) are used. The course is taught by a team of expert practicing and licensed professional engineers. We will be using our online learning management system (LMS). The LMS allows ongoing online communication with the expert instructors throughout the training. As there are no published versions of previous California Traffic Engineer Exams, this course does not represent actual problems that could appear in the actual exam. But rather, we have included more than 100 sample problems that represent the knowledge that is expected of any transportation engineer practicing Traffic Engineering in California. These sample problems are designed to assist the students in practicing using the reference material. This course is intended as a review course for transportation professionals who already have the requisite education and professional experience to qualify to take the TE licensure exam in California. We assume all examinees have the appropriate knowledge of Traffic Engineering and Transportation Planning and are familiar with all the technical references required by the Board. This course is not a class to teach the topic areas and introduce the use of these references; rather, it is an overall review of topic areas and examples of how to apply the reference materials in solving the TE exam problems efficiently. This course is not designed to teach the fundamentals of Traffic Engineering, which should be learned either in school or at work as part of one's professional experience in Traffic Engineering, but to refresh areas that may be on the exam for the trained professional. Topics IncludeTraffic Impact Analysis Parking Analysis Level of Service & Capacity Geometric Design of Roadways Transportation Facilities Design Traffic Signals and Lighting Traffic Control Devices Bicycles, Pedestrians Facilities Traffic Flow What You Will Learn Students will learn how to prepare for the TE exam and will receive an overview of the subjects covered in the TE exam. Students will also learn techniques to solve exam questions in a short period of time while applying reference materials as listed on the Board's website. For questions about the course content, preparing for the class and/or preparing for the exam, please contact the class coordinator, Afsaneh Yavari (mailto:afsaneh.yavari@berkeley.edu?Subject=Hello%20again). Who Should Attend Transportation professionals preparing for the California Traffic Engineer (TE) licensure exam. Examinees are assumed to have the requisite education and professional experience to qualify to take the California Traffic Engineer Exam. Examinees who may have deficiencies in any of the subjects covered in the CA Traffic Engineer Exam test plan (https://www.bpelsg.ca.gov/applicants/plan_traffic.pdf) may consider taking one or more of our upcoming training classes (https://registration.techtransfer.berkeley.edu/wconnect/ShowSchedule.awp?~~GROUP~:FULL~&Async=OFF&TITLE=Upcoming+Classes), such as the Fundamentals of Traffic Engineering (https://registration.techtransfer.berkeley.edu/wconnect/CourseStatus.awp?&course=2640TE010601). Testimonials from last year's attendees: "What the course excelled at was preparing test takers on navigating the reference material…The exam requires the test taker to know what reference material to look through immediately." "I thought the class was very effective and especially helpful in not only reviewing the technical aspects of traffic engineering, but also feedback on what to expect, tips for test taking, etc. Taking this course was the difference in being able to pass this test the first time, thank you!"

events.title: Stephen Small | Transnational Black culture in Liverpool at the end of the twentieth century: anomalous legacies in the 'slaving capital of the world' aka 'the second city of Empire'
events.description: In the 1950s the Black population (Afro-Caribbean and African) of England was estimated at no more than 50,000; by the 1970s it had increased to 400,000 and by 2001, the census reported it was over 1.1 million. Most research on Black Britain in this period is focused on the population at the center of this increase, the so-called 'Windrush Generation' – that is, West Indian settlers that arrived since the 1940s, developed family units with two West Indian parents, primarily in London, and with limited firsthand experience or collective memory of legacies of slavery and imperialism in England itself. This research is reflected in the work of scholars like Stuart Hall, Paul Gilroy, Hazel Carby, Heidi Mirza and John Solomos. Hall highlighted how 'Black is not a question of pigmentation … [It] is a historical category, a political category, a cultural category'; and Mirza insisted that 'It is only by attention to situated localised accounts of 'marginalised lives' that we can reveal the ways of 'being and becoming' a gendered, sexed, raced and classed subject'. While Black Liverpool shared much in common with Black London and other cities in this period, Liverpool's assemblage of features - what I denote as a racialised anomaly - was markedly different. There were far more Africans than West Indians, more long-term citizens than recent immigrants, the highest proportion of inter-racial marriages and people of mixed racial origins in the nation, more extensive first-hand experiences, and a far more vivid collective memory of imperialism in West Africa. These differences arose from the city's distinctive involvement in slavery and imperialism, the settlement in imperial Liverpool of (overwhelmingly male) seamen from West Africa; and the forced concentration of Black and multi-racial families in one neighbourhood (Liverpool 8 - later known as Toxteth). The city historically also had a far greater reliance on port activities and consistently higher rates of unemployment than in any other English city. In this presentation, drawing in his recently published book – Black Liverpool: 'the real thing' - Professor Stephen Small will examine how the historical and structural features of Black Liverpool gave rise to unique configurations of Black cultural expression in that city in the final decades of the twentieth century. Specifically, how the Black community in Liverpool pursued, embraced and transformed waves of transnational Black culture from West Africa, the West Indies and the United States in the final three decades of the twentieth century. The role of gender ideologies, institutional practices and the agency and experiences of Black women are closely examined. One implication of this study is that an analysis of Black Britain based on a London-centered account of the so-called 'Windrush Generation' is unrepresentative and misleading.Stephen Small is a Professor of the Graduate School in the Department of African American and African Diaspora Studies at the University of California, Berkeley, a position he began in January 2025 after he retired from 30 years teaching on campus. He researches the history and sociology of Black people across the diaspora, with a primary focus on legacies of slavery and imperialism, public history and collective memory. He is a faculty member of the Black Europe Summer School (BESS) (since 2007) – a two-week program in Amsterdam, founded and directed for Dr. Kwame Nimako; and has held visiting positions at universities in Brazil, England, France, Japan, the Netherlands, Spain, and Zimbabwe. He was Guest Curator at the Merseyside Maritime Museum's Atlantic Slave Trade Gallery (now the International Slavery Museum) in Liverpool that opened in 1994. His most recent book is Black Liverpool: 'The real thing' West African, West Indian and Afro-American Culture at the end of the twentieth century published by Liverpool University Press in June 2026. Recent publications include In the Shadows of the Big House: Twenty-First Century Antebellum SlaveCabins and Heritage Tourism in Louisiana (2023) and 1981- Black Liverpool, Past and Present (2022) (co-written with Jimi Jagne). He is also co-editor (with Darlene Clark Hine and Trica Danielle Keaton) of Black Europe and the African Diaspora (2009). Stephen earned his Ph.D. in Sociology at the University of California, Berkeley (1989); his MS.C in Social Sciences from the University of Bristol (1983); and his B.A. (honours) in Economics and Sociology from the University of Kent at Canterbury (1979). Stephen was born and raised in Liverpool, England – the city with the nation's longest-standing Black population. events.title: Berkeley Art, Law, and Finance Project: Hidden Layers: AI Infrastructures and Hallucinations Opening Reception
events.organizer: Berkeley Art, Law, and Finance Project
events.description: Co-sponsored by the Berkeley Art, Law, and Finance Project, Hidden Layers brings together international artists working at the intersection of contemporary art and machine learning to make visible the layers of artificial intelligence that normally stay out of sight: among them, its planetary infrastructure, its ideological biases, its unexpected outputs. Taking the “hidden layers” of neural networks as its conceptual frame, the exhibition asks what AI conceals and what it invents, foregrounding the hallucinations, biases, and latent spaces through which these systems generate images, texts, and worlds. Participating artists include Nouf Aljowaysir, Gašper Beguš, Nina Beguš & Metahaven, Grégory Chatonsky, Jill Miller & Asma Kazmi, Greg Niemeyer, Mario Santamaria & Alex Saum-Pascual, and more to be announced. events.title: Casual Conversation with Venerable Pomnyun Sunim
events.location: Sutardja Dai Hall, Banatao Auditorium, Room 310, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker: Venerable Pomnyun Sunim (Korean Seon (Zen) Buddhist monk) In Person Event | RSVP Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Note: This event will begin exactly at the scheduled time of 4:00 PM. Talk Summary: How can we live with greater clarity, resilience, and compassion in a rapidly changing world? In this interactive "Casual Conversation," Venerable Pomnyun Sunim invites students and community members to openly explore questions about stress, relationships, career uncertainty, emotional wellbeing, social conflict, and the search for meaning in modern life. Known for his practical and accessible teaching style, Venerable Pomnyun Sunim responds directly to audience questions with insight, humor, and compassion. Rather than offering abstract religious doctrine, he shares practical wisdom grounded in Buddhist philosophy and decades of humanitarian and social engagement. The conversation may also touch on broader topics including mindfulness, sustainable living, peacebuilding, social responsibility, and how individuals can contribute positively to society while maintaining inner balance and freedom. This event is open to people of all backgrounds, beliefs, and levels of familiarity with Buddhism. Speaker Bio: Venerable Pomnyun Sunim is a highly respected Korean Seon (Zen) Buddhist monk, humanitarian leader, author, and founder of Jungto Society, an international volunteer-based organization dedicated to spiritual practice, social engagement, environmental sustainability, and peacebuilding. He is widely recognized for his accessible and deeply engaging public dialogues known as "Casual Conversations" (즉문즉설), where he responds spontaneously to audience questions about everyday life challenges. His teachings focus on practical wisdom, emotional clarity, compassion, and personal responsibility, making them highly relevant across cultural, academic, and professional communities. Venerable Pomnyun Sunim has delivered talks and interactive sessions at leading academic institutions including Harvard University, Columbia University, UCLA, Johns Hopkins University, the University of Toronto, and other universities across North America and Asia. He has also spoken with professionals at organizations such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Bank, and global technology companies including Google. In 2002, he received the Ramon Magsaysay Award, often regarded as Asia's Nobel Prize, in recognition of his humanitarian work, peacebuilding efforts, and contributions to socially engaged Buddhism.

events.title: BPM 210 Building Trust
events.description: Due to the pre-work required, access to registration is disabled one week prior to the event. This 4.5-hour workshop is part of the BPM Part 3: Grow Your Team series and is an elective option for the UC Systemwide People Management Certificate. In this highly interactive workshop, each participant's experience is drawn upon for the learning. Ideally, to contribute to and enhance understanding, participants will come with current and/or previous people management experience. Trust is at the heart of every relationship, and it's especially critical in the workplace. In fact, the primary factor affecting employee turnover is whether or not a trusting relationship was developed between the manager and the employee. This workshop teaches how to build trust to increase engagement, creativity, and commitment. Based on 30 years of research, The Ken Blanchard Companies have developed a simple, yet powerful, trust model that provides a common language and framework, focused on the specific behaviors that build trust. By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to: *Describe the impact of behaviors on building and eroding trust *Identify aspects that need attention to build and maintain trusting relationships *Use tools to improve, or even rebuild trust when it is broken *Maintain a safe environment where employees know their leaders mean them no harm

events.title: Construction Inspection of Traffic Signals
events.description: Description Traffic signal construction is a critical component of roadway infrastructure that demands precision, adherence to standards, and proactive oversight. For inspectors, construction managers, and traffic engineers, success depends not only on understanding how systems are built but also on recognizing when installation deviates from plans, specifications, or best practices. Minor issues such as improper wiring, inadequate grounding, or ineffective traffic control can introduce safety risks, trigger costly rework, and increase agency liability. This intensive online course is designed to prepare participants for what they will encounter in the field when overseeing traffic signal construction. While the course does not focus on signal design, it provides essential exposure to design elements from an inspector's and owner's perspective. It is intended to help participants understand how design intent is translated into constructed systems and how to verify that the work is completed correctly, safely, and in compliance with Caltrans Standard Plans and Specifications. Participants can expect practical, field-oriented instructions on inspecting and evaluating key signal system components, including conductors and cables, signal heads, controller cabinets, grounding systems, and pedestrian and vehicle detection technologies. The course also emphasizes plan interpretation at a level appropriate for oversight roles. Participants will learn what to look for in the plans, how to identify inconsistencies, and how to apply sufficient technical understanding to assess compliance without performing design work. In addition, the course addresses coordination with contractors, construction documentation, and communication practices that support CIP delivery and protect agencies throughout project implementation. Through real-world case studies, participants will gain insight into common construction challenges, effective inspection strategies, and documentation approaches that stand up to scrutiny. Led by experienced industry professionals, this course equips inspectors, construction managers, and traffic engineers with the practical knowledge and judgment needed to confidently oversee traffic signal construction by bridging the gap between design intent and successful field execution. Topics IncludeSignal Plan Interpretation & Pre-Construction Activities Reading and understanding traffic signal plans Site assessments and preparatory inspections Electrical and Structural Installation Electrical service installation procedures Standards for pedestals, posts, and mounting hardware Bonding and grounding requirements Conduit and Cabling Systems Conduit installation and layout Cable splicing and termination Pull box installation and accessibility Traffic Signal Components Installation of signal heads, brackets, and supporting appurtenances Vehicle and pedestrian detector systems Pedestrian Safety & Americans with Disability Act (ADA) Signal controller cabinet assembly and configuration Construction Close-Out & Asset Management Maintenance considerations during and after construction Salvage and reuse of components Integration of new technology and smart signal components What You Will Learn By attending this class, participants will gain a comprehensive understanding of the full lifecycle of traffic signal construction-from interpreting signal plans and preparing for construction, to installing electrical systems, conduit, and signal components. Attendees will learn industry best practices for ensuring proper bonding, grounding, and splicing, as well as techniques for setting up signal heads, controllers, and detection systems. The course also covers maintenance strategies, salvage procedures, and the integration of modern signal technologies. Through this training, attendees will be equipped with the practical knowledge and field-based insights necessary to effectively inspect, manage, and support the delivery of safe and compliant traffic signal projects. Who Should Attend Ideal for traffic signal technicians, engineering inspectors, electrical contractors, junior engineers, and traffic signal engineers involved in the design, oversight, or inspection of signal infrastructure projects.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Debarati Sanyal
events.description: Arts of the Border (Fordham, 2025) investigates the consequences of unfolding catastrophes across the world and the displacement they continue to produce. Through recent narratives and media representations of the refugee "crisis" at Europe's edges, it tells a new story about those on the move, the technologies unleashed on them at borders, the racialized and colonial histories that inform these technologies, and the artistry with which migrants and allies bear witness to displacement. The book reorients us toward the creativity and movement of migrants themselves — their "arts of the border" — as well as toward the political force of the arts that represent them, whether in literature, documentary film, or art installations.Debarati Sanyal (French) proposes kino-aesthetics as a framework for capture and fugitivity at borders. From kino (to set in motion) and aesthetics (relating to sensory perception), kino-aesthetics conveys the force of bodies in motion and the image in its circulation. Sanyal examines the simultaneity of capture and escape at thresholds of illegalization, from airport detention zones to Calais's "jungle" and the Euro-African border at Ceuta and Melilla. What emerges throughout these case studies is a portrayal of border violence in its racial and colonial forms as well as an archive of refusal, fugitivity, and un-bordered imagining. Sanyal is joined by Damon Young (Film & Media and French). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

Drawing from research in neonatal and anesthesia care environments, we will explore how wearable sensing can objectively characterize clinical performance in high-risk healthcare settings. The talk will highlight how these approaches can support both patient safety and clinician occupational safety through data-driven training, human factors analysis, and improved understanding of healthcare work.

events.title: (Screening) Gaavani | Celebrating the Female Voice in Gurbani Kirtan
events.description: Join us for a screening of Gaavani (https://www.gaavani.com/), a documentary that marks a significant moment in Sikh history. For the first time in 556 years since the founding of the Sikh faith, 31 women travel across India to sing kirtan in all 31 primary musical raags of the Guru Granth Sahib at sacred sites. More than a documentary, Gaavani (https://www.gaavani.com/) is a cinematic reclamation of women's spiritual leadership, inheritance, and presence within the sacred tradition of kirtan. The screening will be followed by a conversation with filmmaker Navpreet Kaur (https://www.gaavani.com/). The event will be moderated by Puninder Singh (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/people/puninder-singh), the Sabharwal Lecturer in Sikh Studies at UC Berkeley. ————���DATE: Thu, September 17, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall —————-SYNOPSIS:Gaavani (https://www.gaavani.com/) follows a diverse group of 31 women—teachers, students, mothers, and community members—as they journey across India to perform kirtan in the 31 primary raags of the Guru Granth Sahib. From the busy streets of Delhi to historic shrines in Amritsar and beyond, the film captures both the challenges and triumphs of this groundbreaking effort. The documentary explores the relationship between ritual, music, gender, and lived spiritual experience. Featuring insights from scholars and speakers such as Dr. Gurnam Singh and Jessi Kaur, Gaavani reflects on the "female orientation" of the soul in Sikh philosophy and highlights the deep spiritual significance of sung devotion. The film also honors the role of male mentors and allies who supported this movement, presenting a vision of a community in which women and men are empowered to participate fully in the Guru's Shabad. As a legacy project, Gaavani (https://www.gaavani.com/) seeks to inspire Sikh children and adults to discover their own musical connection to Gurbani Kirtan and to help ensure that this sacred art form continues to thrive for future generations. Running time 45 minutes. See the trailer HERE (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pyeqlAeNi9Q) About the Filmmaker:Navpreet Kaur (https://www.gaavani.com/) is a dedicated community leader and media producer based in the San Francisco Bay Area. As a key founder of Gaavani (https://www.gaavani.com/), she has spearheaded global and local initiatives to raise the female voice in Gurbani Kirtan. With a background in project leadership and a passion for deep personal discovery, Navpreet coordinated the historic 31-women Kirtan tour of India and served as the visionary and driving force behind the documentary production. Her work focuses on bridging Sikh spiritual wisdom and traditions with modern and meaningful community, educational and media platforms.About the moderator:Puninder Singh (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/people/puninder-singh) completed his PhD in Linguistic Anthropology at the University of Michigan in 2024. His work broadly examines how language and ideas about language mediate religious experience, particularly in the Sikh tradition. His current work examines the development of a new Sikh intellectual formation between 1920-1940, after the era of the Singh Sabha reform movement. He is also at work on several projects that examine how the Sikh tradition has engaged in dialogic and interactive relations with those around it, both linguistically and otherwise, in the long durée, from the early modern through the contemporary period. He is currently the Sabharwal Lecturer in Sikh Studies at the University of California, Berkeley.Event Poster TBA —————— Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley)PARKING INFORMATION (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/parking-around-campus)Please note that parking in not always easily available in Berkeley. Take public transportation if possible or arrive early to secure your spot.DIRECTIONS (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/contactsdirections) We are located at 10 Stephens Hall on UC Berkeley's campus. Please click this Google Maps Link (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+Berkeley,+CA/@37.8712099,-122.3278764,12z/data=!4m9!4m8!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952!3e0) and enter your point of departure.

events.title: Ariel Tang | Scripting Silence: Animals Political and Unpolitical in Charlotte Beradt's Dreamscape
events.description: This talk features the implicit dialogue between the German-Jewish journalist Charlotte Beradt (1907-1986) and her fellow émigré, Hannah Arendt, regarding the boundaries between humans and animals, as well as the ethical limits of anthropocentrism during political crises. Beradt's Third Reich of Dreams, a catalogue of dreams compiled between 1933 and 1939 on the basis of dreams retold by more than fifty Germans living under totalitarian rule, prompts her readers to re-evaluate the unique traits of physiological activities such as dreaming—as opposed to discursive reasoning—in safeguarding the humane promise of politics. While conventional pictures of human nature often fall prey to naturalistic or essentialist tendencies, the vital dialogue between Beradt and Arendt helps to resuscitate the unmistakable normative value of anthropological evidence, the substance of which often escapes the immediate capture of language and yet preserves the hope for political renewal lost in effable experience. Ariel Tang is a Postdoctoral Fellow in the Department of Political Science at Stanford University. Her research focuses on Enlightenment political thought and its legacies, with special attention to questions related to knowledge institutions, education, and the interactions between culture and nature. Her current book manuscript traces an entangled history of the idea of Bildung and the rise of the modern research university. She received her bachelor's degree in Philosophy from Barnard College, Columbia University, and her PhD in Political Science from Yale University. events.title: CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Susan Murphy: Online Reinforcement Learning for Digital Health Interventions in the Dyadic Setting
events.description: Please join us for a joint CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Susan Murphy Online Reinforcement Learning for Digital Health Interventions in the Dyadic Setting Abstract We present our ongoing work on the development of an online reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that personalizes delivery of interventions sequentially, over time, to members of a dyad. The RL algorithm is one component in the design of the digital health intervention. Different RL components target different elements of the dyad; these elements are a target individual, a carepartner and their relationship. The RL algorithm is a multi-agent RL algorithm in which the 3 agents make decisions on the 3 elements of the dyad. We incorporate domain knowledge in the form of approximal causal directed acyclic graphs to speed up online learning in this sparse data setting. This work is motivated by our development of the ADAPTS-HCT multi-agent RL algorithm, designed to improve medication adherence by young adults who have undergone a blood and bone marrow transplant. The RL algorithm will be deployed in a clinical trial in late summer 2026. BioSusan A. Murphy is Mallinckrodt Professor of Statistics and of Computer Science and Associate Faculty at the Kempner Institute, Harvard University. Her research focuses on improving sequential decision making via the development of online, real-time reinforcement learning algorithms. Her lab is involved in multiple deployments of these algorithms in digital health. She is a member of the US National Academy of Sciences and of the US National Academy of Medicine. In 2013 she was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship for her work on experimental designs to inform sequential decision making. She is a Fellow of the College on Problems in Drug Dependence, Past-President of Institute of Mathematical Statistics, Past-President of the Bernoulli Society and a former editor of the Annals of Statistics. CLIMB Voleon Seminars are organized by the Center for the Theoretical Foundations of Learning, Inference, Information, Intelligence, Mathematics, and Microeconomics at Berkeley (CLIMB), and are generously supported by the Voleon Group. CLIMB addresses new conceptual and mathematical challenges arising at the interface between technology, science, and society.If you require an accommodation for effective communication or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Naomi Yamasaki at climb-support@eecs.berkeley.edu (mailto:naomiy@berkeley.edu) or 510-710-8488 with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: MBN Seminar: Identification of Novel Targets to Reverse Hepatic Fibrogenesis
events.description: Dr. Jennifer Y. Chen, Associate Professor, Department of Medicine, Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, UC San Francisco Dr. Jennifer Y. Chen is a physician-scientist and hepatologist at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF). She completed her medical training at Harvard, where she also pursued postdoctoral research in hepatic stellate cell biology and the molecular mechanisms of liver fibrogenesis. Her research program integrates basic, translational, and clinical investigation to advance precision medicine for patients with chronic liver disease. Focusing on the cellular and molecular pathways that drive hepatic fibrosis, her laboratory is developing novel antifibrotic therapies through collaborations with medicinal chemists to design and optimize small-molecule inhibitors that target key fibrogenic pathways. In parallel, her team is discovering and validating biomarkers that improve the diagnosis, risk stratification, and therapeutic monitoring of patients with liver fibrosis. Her work aims to accelerate the translation of mechanistic discoveries into innovative, personalized treatments that improve outcomes for patients with chronic liver disease.

events.title: Ned Wingreen: Collective dynamics in B cell affinity maturation
events.description: In the humoral immune response, B cells that produce high-affinity antibodies are generated through a Darwinian evolutionary process called affinity maturation. Affinity maturation, which takes place in germinal centers (GC), is driven by cycles of selection (mediated by T cells), division, and hypermutation of B cells. Recently, it was found that the T cells themselves also exhibit dynamic behavior throughout the course of the GC reaction, undergoing affinity-dependent proliferation. A model suggests that this reciprocal stimulation enforces a robust "homeostatic" regulation of the relative number of B cells and T cells in the GC, leading to a constant ratio of GC lymphocytes. But the model also points to a problem: the high mutation rate of GC B cells can lead to "backsliding" of affinity. The proposed solution – a fitness-dependent mutation rate – has been experimentally verified, and has implications beyond B cell affinity maturation.Division(s): INFORMAL SEMINAR

events.title: From Chaebols to Startups to BTS: The Strategic Evolution of Korea's Innovation Ecosystem
events.location: Institute of East Asian Studies, Conference Room, 2111 Bancroft Way, 5th Floor, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker: Yongwook Paik (KAIST) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance - COMING SOON Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: Drawing on insights from the co-authored book The Korean Startup Ecosystem: Past, Present, and Future, this lecture offers an insider's perspective on Korea's evolving innovation landscape. It traces the nation's transition from a conglomerate-driven growth model to an innovation-led economy, highlighting the critical interplay between venture capital, government policy, conglomerates, and entrepreneurial culture. The talk demonstrates how Korea's global cultural powerhouses—including K-pop, K-dramas, and K-beauty—are strategic outcomes of this systematically built ecosystem. Through a comparative lens, the lecture examines the institutional features that distinguish the Korean and U.S. markets across key dimensions like financing, risk tolerance, and policy intervention. It concludes by outlining strategic implications for global founders, investors, and policymakers, followed by an interactive Q&A session. Speaker Bio: Professor Paik is a tenured professor at the KAIST College of Business and an affiliated professor at the KAIST College of AI. His research explores the intersection of entrepreneurship, innovation, strategy, institutions, and public policy. He serves as an editorial review board member and referee for numerous top-tier academic journals in his field, and his research has appeared in premier publications such as the Strategic Management Journal, Organization Science, Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal, and the Journal of Economics & Management Strategy. Before joining KAIST in 2018, Professor Paik served as an assistant professor at the University of Southern California's Marshall School of Business and Washington University in St. Louis's Olin Business School. He holds a Ph.D. in Economics from the University of California, Berkeley. Prior to his academic career, he was a patent attorney at the leading South Korean law firm Kim & Chang, advising both multinational corporations and entrepreneurial ventures. A seasoned advisor in the innovation ecosystem, Professor Paik cofounded the venture capital firm TBW Investment, which was later acquired via M&A. He is a Board Member of Hanyang Eng Co., a major KOSDAQ-listed semiconductor and high-tech facility engineering firm, and currently serves as a policy advisor to South Korea's National Economic Advisory Council.

events.title: Julia Nelsen | Translation as Rediscovery: Introducing Fausta Cialente
events.description: Fausta Cialente (1898-1994) was one of Italy's most significant twentieth-century authors. Though she won critical acclaim—albeit late in her career—Cialente remained overlooked for decades until the recent rerelease of her literary works in Italian. A Very Cold Winter (Transit Books, 2026) is the first of Cialente's novels to be rediscovered in translation by Julia Nelsen. In conversation with Professor Mairi McLaughlin, Nelsen will discuss her translation of A Very Cold Winter, situate Cialente within the broader landscape of modern Italian and international literature, and explore the role translators play in recovering unsung voices.Julia Nelsen translates between English and Italian. In addition to her work on Fausta Cialente, her essays and translations have appeared in journals including Circumference, Two Lines,Firmament, and the Chicago Review. Alongside translation, she currently serves as policy analyst for the UCLA Academic Senate, and previously taught writing and literature courses and managed international partnerships between Europe and the West Coast. She holds a PhD in Comparative Literature from UC Berkeley and a Masters in European languages from the University of Milan.Mairi McLaughlin is Professor and Chair in the Department of French and an Affiliated Member of the Departments of Linguistics and Italian Studies at UC Berkeley. She specializes in French/Romance Linguistics and in Translation Studies and has published extensively on language contact, the language of the media, and journalistic and literary translation. Her books have been published by Garnier, Legenda, and Oxford University Press, and she has published articles in journals such as French Studies, The Italianist, Langages, META, Perspectives, and Target.If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: Synchro and SimTraffic for Signal Coordination
events.description: Description This four-session online course (4 hours per session) provides beginning-to-intermediate training in Synchro and SimTraffic software and the recently published Highway Capacity Manual (HCM) 7th Edition: A Guide for Multimodal Mobility Analysis (TRB 2022 and HCS7). Using a combination of interactive lecture, question and answer, and virtual computer lab, you will become proficient in the network coding and use of Synchro and SimTraffic for signal optimization and coordination projects. Working on a real-world multi-modal project, students will use Synchro to incorporate a Bing aerial background, add/modify roadways, input intersection geometrics, enter multi-modal traffic volumes (cars, trucks, pedestrians, and bicycles), and signal timings to replicate / validate existing operations for signalized and unsignalized intersections and roundabouts. Students will also use Synchro to evaluate and develop optimal signal timing plans that reduce delays, stops, congestion, fuel consumption, and greenhouse gas emissions. The seamless integration of Synchro with SimTraffic, a microsimulation software, will be used to evaluate intersection operations and compare the differences between "isolated - macro-level" Synchro and "network-wide - micro-level" SimTraffic analysis that is recommended for multi-modal, closely spaced intersections and congested corridors. Lastly, this course will teach you how to review and understand the potential differences in delay, level of service, and queuing analysis when using the empirical (Synchro) analysis or the micro-simulation (SimTraffic) analysis. Topics IncludeDetailed review of Synchro input requirements Developing a Synchro network for a real-world multi-modal project Analysis of signalized, unsignalized and roundabout intersections using Synchro Multi-modal vehicle, pedestrian and bicycle LOS using HCM 7th Edition Optimizing signal timings for a single intersection that is added to an existing corridor Optimizing signal timings for a group of intersections Seemless Integration of SYNCHRO with SimTraffic SimTraffic Model Calibration and Application What You Will Learn Using a real-world project in a virtual computer lab class setting, students will be able to interact with the instructor as they learn how to develop a network and use the Synchro and SimTraffic software. This includes incorporating a Bing aerial background, add/modify straight and curved roadways, inputting intersection geometrics and pocket lengths, entering multi-modal volumes (cars, trucks, peds, and bicyclists), and signal timings to replicate / validate existing operations analysis for signalized and unsignalized intersections and roundabouts. You will learn the steps used to optimize and coordinate a group of intersections to reduce delays, stops, congestion, fuel consumption, and greenhouse gas emissions. Lastly, you will learn how to review and understand the analysis results and the potential differences when using the empirical (Synchro) analysis or the micro-simulation (SimTraffic) analysis for signal coordination projects. The materials in this course are based on the following references:Transportation Research Board. Highway Capacity Manual, 7th Edition, 2022 CUBIC Transportation Systems. Synchro Studio 12 Traffic Signal Software -User Guide, 2024 Who Should Attend No prior experience using Synchro and SimTraffic is necessary. This course is designed for traffic engineers, planners, and technicians in both public agencies and private firms who engage in improving signal system optimization and coordination projects using the integrated Optimization Module in the Synchro software.

events.title: Robert G. Strand | Nordic Capitalism: Lessons for Realizing Sustainable Capitalism
events.description: Why do the Nordics consistently rank among the world's happiest, most prosperous, and most trusted societies? What lessons might the Nordics offer the United States at a moment when many people feel growing frustration and anxiety about the direction of American capitalism?Nordic Capitalism: Lessons for Realizing Sustainable Capitalism (2026, Cambridge University Press; open access:https://bit.ly/3MSvrOp (https://bit.ly/3MSvrOp)) by Robert G. Strand explores a simple but urgent idea: capitalism must be rooted in democracy if it is to support freedom, shared prosperity, and sustainability. Drawing on research, lived experience, and comparative analysis between the Nordics and the United States, Strand argues that the Nordic countries offer practical inspiration for reimagining capitalism in the twenty-first century. "Where democracy is in charge of capitalism, the people win. When capitalism is in charge of democracy, the oligarchs win. In this important book, Robert G. Strand shows how democracies can stay in charge. Nordic Capitalism explains that the Nordic nations can be a model for the US, and how democratic capitalism serves the many, not the few." — Robert B. Reich, Former U.S. Secretary of Labor and Professor Emeritus of Public Policy, UC Berkeley Dr. Robert G. Strand is the founding Executive Director of the Nordic Center at UC Berkeley and Executive Director of the Center for Responsible Business at Berkeley Haas, where he serves on the faculty. He is also Associate Professor at Copenhagen Business School. His research examines how Nordic societies have organized capitalism and how companies pursue responsible and sustainable business, with attention to applications for reimagining American capitalism. Before joining UC Berkeley in 2014, he served as Assistant Professor at Copenhagen Business School following a decade in corporate America with IBM and Boston Scientific. He received a Ph.D. in Corporate Social Responsibility from Copenhagen Business School, an MBA in International Business from the University of Minnesota, and a B.S. in Industrial Engineering from the University of Wisconsin. He was a U.S. Fulbright Scholar to Norway at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Thomas Farber
events.description: Describing America's deeply unsettling current politics, at age eighty-one Thomas Farber (English) explores personal accountability, impending second childhoods, mortality, and the hunger for immortality. Weighing the functions of satire and the meaning of art, his short takes illuminate, debunk, commiserate, and celebrate by rejoinder.Reckonings (El León Literary Arts/Manoa Books, 2026) is framed by two insights: no one chooses to be born, and no one can help being what they are. Reckoning with democracy in crisis, aging and mortality, his career, the role of the writer, and the fate of books, Farber reflects on endings with curiosity, honesty, wit, and compassion. Reckonings is the latest in a series of remarkable creative memoirs he has written over the past decade, coming to terms with life and its limits. Farber is joined by Sam Otter (English). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: Carla Shatz & Corey Goodman Lectureship Series with Dr. Erin Schuman
events.description: The Department of Neuroscience and the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute (HWNI) are delighted to announce the 2026 Carla Shatz & Corey Goodman Lectureship Series. This event, created through the generosity of co-founding directors of the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute, Dr. Carla Shatz and Dr. Corey Goodman, will bring outstanding neuroscientists to our campus to share their research and engage with our vibrant, interdisciplinary scientific community, spanning the full breadth of mind and brain science. This year's guest speaker will be Dr. Erin M. Schuman (https://brain.mpg.de/schuman), former Professor and Director of the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research in Frankfurt, Germany, and now Director of University College London Queen Square Institute of Neurology. The Schuman lab's long-standing research interest is the study of cellular mechanisms and neural circuits that underlie information processing and storage. The lab focuses on the molecular and cell biological processes that control protein synthesis and degradation in neurons and their synapses. The complex morphology of neurons, with most synapses located hundreds of microns from the cell body, presents a logistical challenge for the establishment, maintenance and modification of local synaptic proteomes. For her groundbreaking work on local protein translation in neurons and the establishment of its importance for brain development and plasticity, Dr. Schuman has been awarded the 2026 Kavli Prize in Neuroscience (https://www.kavliprize.org/bio/erin-schuman). Join us for an inspiring afternoon of conversation and meaningful connections as we delve into the latest advances in neuroscience.

events.title: Vaṭivam: The Work of Form in Tamil Narrative Cultures | A Conference in Tamil Studies
events.description: The Berkeley Tamil Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/language/berkeley-tamil-initiative) is pleased to present The Work of Form in Tamil Narrative Cultures (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/language/tamilberkeley/uc-berkeley-conference-tamil-studies), a Tamil Studies conference exploring vaṭivam—form, shape, style, arrangement, and embodiment—as a way to understand how Tamil narratives are created, circulated, and transformed across literature, performance, visual culture, cinema, and digital media. More than a neutral vessel for narrative, vaṭivam offers a way to understand form as an aesthetic practice, a material structure, and a response to changing social worlds. Bringing together scholars working across literature, performance, visual culture, cinema, and digital media, the conference will examine how Tamil narrative forms have been made and remade across time. By placing premodern and modern materials in conversation, The Work of Form in Tamil Narrative Cultures (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/language/tamilberkeley/uc-berkeley-conference-tamil-studies) asks how Tamil traditions can contribute to broader debates on form, media, and circulation, while remaining attentive to the histories, languages, and material contexts that shape Tamil cultural production. Conference led by Vasugi Kailasam (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/vasugi-kailasam), Assistant Professor of Tamil Studies in the Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. events.title: Roadway Geometric Design in California
events.description: Description This dynamic three-day, in-person course provides a deep dive into the principles and best practices of roadway geometric design in California. Built for professionals looking to strengthen or refresh their roadway design knowledge and expertise, the course begins with the latest transportation planning perspectives and emerging multimodal design philosophies that prioritize safety, mobility, and accessibility for all road users. Students will work directly with the industry's most essential design resources, including the Caltrans Highway Design Manual (HDM), the AASHTO Greenbook, PROWAG, the 2026 California MUTCD, and other key state, federal, and local guidelines. Through real world examples, students will learn how to apply geometric design principles to evaluate constraints, solve design challenges, and develop context sensitive solutions for various design projects. This fast-paced, interactive course blends expert instruction, case studies, group problem solving, and hands-on exercises modeled on real projects. Students are expected to have prior knowledge of or experience with geometric design of roadways, and familiarity with the HDM, AASHTO, and CA MUTCD. Key Topics IncludeGeometric Design Basics & Planning Context Modern Design Philosophy for All Users Design Standards & Guidance (HDM, AASHTO, NACTO, PROWAG, CAMUTCD) Traffic Operations: LOS, Capacity, and VMT Roadway Segment Design (Cross Sections, Profiles, Drainage, Superelevation) Horizontal & Vertical Curve Design Sight Distance Fundamentals (Stopping, Passing, Intersection, Ped/Bike) Intersection Design (Radii, Turn Pockets, Curb Ramps, Signals, Roundabouts) Bikeway Design (Class I-IV Facilities) Pedestrian Facilities Design & Accessibility (ADA/PROWAG) Temporary Traffic Control & Work Zone Design Freeway Design Elements (Interchanges, Merge/Diverge, Mainline) What You Will Learn Students will gain a strong understanding of the principles and best practices of geometric design across multiple roadway functional classes, along with the external factors that influence design decisions. Who Should Attend This course is intended for transportation engineers and technicians who have some basic prior knowledge of or experience with geometric design of roadways, as well as for those more experienced who seek a refresher course. Requirements A laptop computer is not required but is encouraged for group exercises and individual break-out sessions. Participants should bring a pencil, pen, notebook, and engineer's scale for in-class exercises, and are encouraged to print out the course materials (electronic PDF to be provided) prior to the class.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Diego Pirillo
events.description: The Atlantic Republic of Letters (Pennsylvania, 2026) offers an alternative intellectual history of early America. Focusing on Benjamin Franklin's Philadelphia, the book frames Euro-American colonialism as an intellectual enterprise, established not only through military and economic means but also through books, ideas, and cultural institutions. Through extensive archival research, Diego Pirillo (Italian) brings together two interconnected histories. First, he recovers the place of British America in the cosmopolitan world of the Republic of Letters, studying the communication system that facilitated the transatlantic circulation of knowledge. Second, he shows that knowledge was weaponized in the effort to survey and control North America. While fashioning themselves as independent and cosmopolitan scholars, Franklin and his associates were in fact deeply tied to political power and tailored their ideas to the needs of their patrons. They served as agents of empire and helped to devise and put into practice the colonial project. Not only were books, libraries, and cultural institutions funded by the wealth created by the slave trade and the expropriation of Indigenous land, but, as Pirillo argues, the very taxonomies and classification systems that Euro-American scholars devised directly shaped the colonial enterprise. The Atlantic Republic of Letters illuminates the relationship among books, intellectuals, and colonial governance, and explores the ways in which knowledge circulated and shaped conquest. Pirillo is joined by Brian DeLay (History). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: Tang Music in Contemporary China: Sensing Artistry Through Time
events.description: Tang Music in Contemporary China: Sensing Artistry Through Time October 8 Keynote Lecture (125 Morrison Hall) October 9 (125 Morrison Hall) October 10 (Hertz Hall)— Full program will be available later this spring — The resplendent court-entertainment music of the Tang dynasty (618–907 CE), born from cultural exchange along the early Silk Road, has always loomed large in histories of Chinese music. But in today's China, reconstructive performances of this music have begun to assert its place — as living, breathing performance art — in concert halls and social media feeds, too. This conference brings together scholars and performers from across the world, including leading and emerging experts from China, to present, evaluate, and propel forward global scholarly and artistic discourse on Tang music in the contemporary world. Papers will explore the material culture of the Silk Road, early notations and musical instruments, techniques of historical reconstruction and performance, and the place of historical music and dance in contemporary Chinese society. Three leading ensembles from China and the United States will give live performances of Tang music and dance, followed by a roundtable discussion bringing scholarship and performance into critical dialogue.

events.title: 2026 Feldman Lecture | Reckoning with the Past in Germany and the United States: The Case for Thinking Comparatively about Reparative Justice
events.description: German atonement for the Holocaust has been widely hailed by the international community as a paragon of national reckoning, and over the last decade, African American intellectuals such as Ta-Nehisi Coates have explicitly invoked Germany as a useful model in their calls for Americans to confront the legacy of slavery and other forms of state-sanctioned racism. In this lecture, Rita Chin, will trace the complicated, fraught 80-year process by which Germans have dealt with the Nazi past, focusing on developments and debates in the Federal Republic. She will consider the specific ways in which the German case is instructive for Americans seeking to pursue redress but also explore how Germany's vaunted memory culture has become fossilized such that it has sometimes become a stumbling block for a German society struggling to respond to contemporary challenges. Thinking comparatively about how to reckon with legacies of state-sanctioned racial harm, oppression, and violence not only presents Americans with a concrete template for imagining what reparative justice might look like, Chin suggests, it may also help Germans acknowledge the shape-shifting aspects of racism and perhaps even rethink some of the outdated aspects of their memory culture. Rita Chin, Louise A. Tilly Collegiate Professor of European History and Associate Dean of Social Sciences of the Rackham Graduate School at the University of Michigan, is a historian of modern Europe with particular expertise in immigration and human mobility, race and ethnicity, and colonialism and post-colonialism. Trained in European cultural and intellectual history, she has sought to apply these modes of inquiry to her ongoing interest in how difference and diversity have shaped the very terms of modern Germany and Europe more generally. Her research and writing have been supported by the SSRC, the Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars, the ACLS Burkhardt Fellowship for Recently Tenured Scholars, the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, and the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation. events.title: The Significance of Postcolonial Fascism in Cold War Korea
events.location: Institute of East Asian Studies, Conference Room, 2111 Bancroft Way, 5th Floor, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker: Sungik Yang (Arizona State University) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance - COMING SOON Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: The years after Korea's independence from Japanese colonial rule in 1945 were a time of extreme crisis that opened a space for fascist ideologies and discourses to gain ascendancy. In response to national division and political polarization and violence, there arose a heavily nationalist ruling discourse that openly promoted the supremacy of the homogeneous ethnic nation above all competing forms of identity while rejecting core tenets of Western liberalism, containing strong parallels with fascist ideologies in Europe and Japan. Furthermore, this hegemonic discourse pervaded Korean political culture for decades, helping to prop up authoritarian regimes in the country until the 1980s. This discourse, which I call "transcendent nationalism," was a product of the intersection of Korea's postcolonial and Cold War conditions. It sought to overcome Cold War divisions through an embrace of the Korean nation while maintaining colonial-era suspicions of Western capitalist modernity. Ultimately, the fascistic aspects of South Korea's post-1945 political culture reveals the liminal position that Koreans found themselves in during the Cold War, being pulled into the U.S.'s anticommunist orbit but expressing discomfort with American political and cultural hegemony. In addition, postcolonial Korea emerges as an intriguing case study to better understand the nature of fascism as a political discourse promoting an alternative form of modernity that rejected those of capitalist liberalism and communism. By analyzing how fascism took root in a postcolonial nation-state after World War II, we can also gain an understanding of fascism's enduring appeal in global politics even today. Speaker Bio: Sungik Yang is an assistant professor of history at Arizona State University. He is a political and intellectual historian of modern Korea, focusing on political ideology, nationalism, democracy, and historical memory. His forthcoming book is titled Nation Transcendent: Postcolonial Fascism in Cold War Korea.

events.title: Vistro for Traffic Studies
events.description: Description This 8-hour online course (4 hours per session) provides beginning-to-intermediate training in developing and/or reviewing traffic studies completed using the VISTRO software developed by PTV / Umovity. Using a combination of interactive lecture, question and answer, and hands-on computer lab VISTRO model development, you will become proficient in the VISTRO Traffic Impact Study (TIS) software, including defining a project's vehicle trip generation (residential, office, industrial or mixed-use), trip distribution and trip assignment using a real-world project. Students will learn how to use VISTRO to conduct industry standards using the Highway Capacity Manual 7th Edition: A Guide for Multimodal Mobility Analysis (TRB 2022 and HCS7) analysis for vehicles, pedestrians, and bicyclists, and level of service analysis for signalized, unsignalized and roundabout intersections. Students will also learn how to review VISTRO completed traffic impact study parameters, including geometrics (using the integrated Google aerials and street-view), multi-modal volumes, and signal timing inputs (including Leading Pedestrian Intervals). Lastly, students will be introduced to VISSIM, the microsimulation software that is a separate and integrated microsimulation software also developed by PTV / Umovity. VISSIM is used to fully analyze corridor intersection microsimulation operations, and we will compare the primary differences between "isolated - macro-level" VISTRO and "network-wide - micro-level" VISSIM analysis. Topics IncludeDetailed review of VISTRO Traffic Impact Study (TIS) Model input requirements Development of VISTRO network using a hands-on real-world multi-modal project Analysis of signalized, unsignalized and roundabout intersections using VISTRO Multi-modal vehicle, pedestrian, and bicycle LOS using the HCM 7th Edition Quality Assurance / Quality Control (QA/QC) of VISTRO Results Introduction to VISSIM, an integrated microsimulation software What You Will Learn Using a hands-on real-world project in a virtual computer lab class setting, students will be able to interact with the instructor as they become proficient in the VISTRO Traffic Impact Study (TIS) software. This includes defining a project vehicle trip generation (residential, office, industrial or mixed-use), trip distribution and assignment. Students will also learn how to review VISTRO completed traffic impact study parameters, including geometrics, multi-modal volumes, and signal timing inputs (including Leading Pedestrian Intervals). You will learn the steps to effectively Quality Assurance / Quality Control (QA/QC) review VISTRO Traffic Impact Study (TIS) Reports, including the analysis for vehicles, pedestrians, and bicyclists, and level of service analysis for signalized, unsignalized and roundabout intersections. Who Should Attend No prior experience using VISTRO or VISSIM is necessary. This course is designed for traffic engineers, planners, and technicians in both public agencies and private firms who engage in either developing or reviewing Traffic Impact Studies completed using the VISTRO Traffic Impact Study (TIS) software. The materials in this course are based on the following references:PTV Group - VISTRO software (2025), PTV Group - Modeling and Planning Manual Transportation Research Board. Highway Capacity Manual,7th Edition, 2022

events.title: Indranil Chakravarty | The Tree Within: Octavio Paz's Years in India.
events.description: A talk by Indranil Chakravarty (https://indrachakra.com/), film historian, screenwriter, and author, on his new book, The Tree Within: Octavio Paz's Years in India (https://0235947a.streak-link.com/C3VGHy6fX8I10Qk1JABJW9Rn/https%3A%2F%2Fwww.amazon.com%2FTree-Within-Mexican-Laureate-Octavio%2Fdp%2F0143471651%2F%3F_encoding%3DUTF8%26pd_rd_w%3DF95xZ%26content-id%3Damzn1.sym.4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%253Aamzn1.symc.5a16118f-86f0-44cd-8e3e-6c5f82df43d0%26pf_rd_p%3D4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%26pf_rd_r%3DVR6CA1607Z5S9X17FJWB%26pd_rd_wg%3Dvlupw%26pd_rd_r%3D12aba704-4be6-41aa-b6f0-8da866b68464%26ref_%3Dpd_hp_d_atf_ci_mcx_mr_ca_hp_atf_d), that explores how Octavio Paz's years as Mexico's ambassador to India transformed his personal life, poetry, philosophy, and understanding of cultural exchange.Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor of Global Modern Art and South and Southeast Asian Art, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley.The Tree Within (https://www.amazon.com/Tree-Within-Mexican-Laureate-Octavio/dp/0143471651/?_encoding=UTF8&pd_rd_w=F95xZ&content-id=amzn1.sym.4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%3Aamzn1.symc.5a16118f-86f0-44cd-8e3e-6c5f82df43d0&pf_rd_p=4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631&pf_rd_r=VR6CA1607Z5S9X17FJWB&pd_rd_wg=vlupw&pd_rd_r=12aba704-4be6-41aa-b6f0-8da866b68464&ref_=pd_hp_d_atf_ci_mcx_mr_ca_hp_atf_d) is the enchanting story of Octavio Paz's passionate love-affair with India where he served as Mexico's ambassador in the 1960s. Immersing himself in the country's rich cultural life and contemplative traditions, Paz travelled widely, forged deep friendships with some of India's finest minds, and produced several of his most inspired poetry and essays. It was here that he met the love of his life and experienced what he called his 'second birth'. In this richly textured and erudite work, Chakravarty reconstructs the inner journey of the poet by delving into multilingual archives, declassified diplomatic files, personal letters, and intimate interviews. Blending biography, cultural history, and literary criticism, The Tree Within is a luminous testament to the enduring alchemy between India and the world through one of the greatest writers of the 20th century.Indranil Chakravarty (https://indrachakra.com/) has taught film history and screenwriting over two decades at film institutes in India and abroad, and has made several documentaries. He studied at Presidency College (Calcutta), Escuela Internacional de Cine y TV (EICTV) in Havana, and earned PhD from Victoria University of Wellington, New Zealand. He has published extensively in international research journals about biopics, literary biography and cosmopolitanism. His earlier book publications include The New Latin American Cinema, India's Audiovisual Market, and one in Spanish titled Redescubriendo a Tagore. events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Diana Martinez
events.description: During US colonial rule in the Philippines, reinforced concrete was used to the near exclusion of all other building materials. In Concrete Colonialism (Duke, 2025), Diana Martinez (Architecture) examines the motivations for and lasting effects of this forgotten colonial policy. Arguing that the pervasive use of reinforced concrete revolutionized techniques of imperial conquest, Martinez shows how concrete reshaped colonialism as a project that sought durable change through the reformation of environments, colonial society, and racialized biologies. Martinez locates the origins of this material revolution in the development of Chicago, highlighting how building this urban center atop exceptionally challenging geology made it possible to transform diverse global ecologies. She details how the material's stability, plasticity, strength, and other qualities served the shifting imperatives of the US colonial regime, playing a central role in defending territory, controlling disease, and constructing monuments to nation and empire. By describing a world irreversibly remade, Martinez urges readers to consider how colonialism persists — in concrete forms — despite claims of its conclusion. Martinez is joined by Matthew Shutzer (History). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: The Dread Heights: Tribulation and Refuge after the Syrian Revolution
events.location: Constance Chiang Pan Anthropology Reading Room, 230 Anthropology and Art Practice Building
events.description: Basit Kareem Iqbal is Associate Professor in the Department of Anthropology and Associate Member in the Department of Religious Studies at McMaster University. An anthropologist and longtime academic editor, his research explores the difficulty of the present within and across distinct traditions and forms of life. Based on fieldwork with refugees, relief workers, and religious scholars in Jordan and Canada, Iqbal's recent monograph The Dread Heights: Tribulation and Refuge after the Syrian Revolution (2025) offers an ethnography of Islamic theology in the shadow of war. He serves on the editorial boards of the journals Critical Times and History of the Present as well as on multiple professional association steering committees. He is currently working on his second monograph, tentatively titled And From What Evil He Created: Essays in Seeking Refuge, and on a translation of Yassin al-Haj Saleh's 2021 book al-Fazi' wa tamthiluh, tentatively titled Representing the Atrocious: On the Destruction of Syria and the Ruination of Form.

events.title: Jürgen Dinkel | All remains in the Family: A History of Inheritance in the US and Europe Since 1800
events.description: Over the next 25 years, Americans will inherit more than $100 trillion. Economists anticipate a "great wealth transfer" from the Baby Boomer generation to their children and grandchildren. At the same time, this enormous wealth will be distributed extremely unevenly throughout society. While a select few will inherit vast fortunes, many will inherit little, nothing at all, or even debt. This raises questions with renewed urgency—questions that have been debated in the transatlantic world since the American and French Revolutions: Who should receive a deceased person's estate? Who counts as family? Who should decide how an estate is distributed? How can the unequal distribution of inherited wealth be justified, and how can the rights to private property and equal opportunities be reconciled? In his lecture, Jürgen Dinkel traces the history of inheritance in the US and Europe since 1800. He demonstrates how governments, families, and individuals repeatedly negotiated the transfer and distribution of estates, thereby also renegotiating kinship relations, the bonds between the individual, the family, and the state, as well as the legitimization of wealth inequalities within their societies. Ultimately, this lecture contributes to the new histories of capitalism, the family, and the state, arguing that Euro-American societies from the 19th to the 21st century are fundamentally structured around inheritance and the family. Jürgen Dinkel is Professor of Modern and Global History at the University of Leipzig. His research focuses on the history of colonialism and decolonization, the Global South in World Politics, and European social history. His most recent publications include: Acknowledgments: The History of Academic Gratitude, in Bulletin of the German Historical Institute, Washington D.C. 76 (Fall 2025); "'The Rich Uncle from America': Transnational Inheritance Transfers between the United States, Germany, and Russia, 1840s–1980s," Law and History Review (2025); and "The Non-Aligned Movement: The Role of Diplomacy in Third-worldism and the Global South," in Oxford Handbook on the History of the Global South (Oxford UP, 2025). events.title: Meeting the Challenges of Transportation Liability and Risk Management
events.description: Description Transportation entities face conflicting and intersecting priorities - they must provide safe, efficient, equitable, multi-modal transportation projects while mitigating financial, legal and operational risk. Legal risk should be addressed by transportation entities early and often, not just after lawsuits have been filed. Employees and officials planning, designing, maintaining and operating their entity's transportation infrastructure need to understand the major legal principles governing roadway litigation. An understanding of the legal statutes, cases, principles and outcomes will help all transportation employees, from engineers, to planners, to maintenance crews understand how to conduct their operations to minimize or reduce legal risk. The intent of this course is to help transportation practitioners understand what claims can be brought against a transportation entity for crashes, how the lawyers representing those entities manage and defend those cases, and how the non-legal transportation professional can actively reduce or manage litigation risks using engineering judgment, proper documentation, and collaboration with legal and non-legal professionals. The training will cover legal concepts related to unsafe condition claims in California, investigation of collisions from a litigation perspective (vs. from a purely operational perspective), and will focus on tort liability litigation practices. This course will cover planning and design elements that provide context sensitive solutions based on the unique geometrics of a given facility while reducing legal risk through proper documentation and engineering judgment. We will discuss legal cases and court decisions that provide the framework for transportation entities to defend against unsafe condition cases. The various defenses available to the transportation entities will be covered, along with practical information for transportation employees to build into their workflow that minimize or reduce legal risk while allowing for creative, innovative design solutions for transportation infrastructure projects. Although the cases discussed will involve lawsuits resulting from highway design, the information provided will help civil engineers involved as witnesses in various types of litigation. Topics Include The course will provide transportation personnel with an understanding of the following:litigation process, including the legal concepts for unsafe condition claims the concept of joint and several liability the available defenses the need for early investigation in some collision cases and the process of providing information (called discovery) during a lawsuit various types of written discovery, oral testimony typically done in these cases, as well as the necessary preparation and assistance needed by employees involved in the litigation matters how to respond to questions from attorneys and become an effective witness in depositions and at trial how to prepare for deposition testimony (and the importance of doing so) how to testify in a trial interaction discussion and pointers on preparing for testimony dispositive motions that can end a case short of a jury several motions, including demurrers, motions to strike, motions for design immunity, and a trial on affirmative defenses explain these motions, and the non-legal transportation official's critical role in successful outcomes to these motions for transportation entities focus on emerging trends in transportation engineering that affect tort liability and risk management. This will include a history of safety programs federally and in California, including the Highway Safety Act, various spot programs, as well as the evolution of corridor safety programs, and the transitions with reactive/proactive safety operations challenges of innovative transportation initiatives when juxtaposed with the tort liability scheme in California What You Will Learn The intent of the course is to improve public agency practices to effectively manage and reduce tort liability. The following learning objectives are primary for this course:Understand the nature of roadway litigation against transportation entities Understand the litigation process in tort liability litigation Familiarize non-legal transportation personnel with the litigation process and their role in that process: Helping them to proactively manage or reduce liability, while Helping the legal team defend litigation matters effectively Help participants with the process of deposition and trial testimony by helping them understand how to approach witness testimony Address current trends in road liability litigation and how those trends can be positively or negatively affected by the transportation employee's work Use real world case examples to teach transportation employees how to use liability neutral documentation Understand the importance of balancing factors in addressing the needs of all road users Who Should Attend This course will benefit transportation professionals (engineers and planners) who work for consultants, cities, counties, and state agencies involved in designing roadway projects. This course is designed for individuals with some background and training in designing streets and intersections who are interested in learning more about tort liability and how it relates to the highway design process. The course may also be helpful to the staff of public agencies who are involved with street and roadway maintenance on a day-to-day basis.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Lisandro Claudio
events.description: In The Profligate Colonial (Cornell, 2025) Lisandro Claudio (South & Southeast Asian Studies) reveals how austerity, long before it became a buzzword of modern technocracy, was a tool of US empire. Austerity is often praised as prudence in hard times, a responsible response to crisis. In the Philippines today, it is treated as common sense, an unquestioned commitment to a strong currency, low inflation, and fiscal restraint. Claudio argues that this orthodoxy is in fact a colonial inheritance — a legacy of American rule that cast Filipinos as reckless spenders and imposed monetary discipline as a civilizing force. At the center of this logic is the "profligate colonial," a feminized, racialized figure who wastes public funds and so requires the steady hand of imperial governance. Focusing on key moments in Philippine economic history across the twentieth century, Claudio charts how austerity was first exported through empire, then domesticated in line with nationalist ambitions. He shows that generations of Filipino policymakers, central bankers, and intellectuals absorbed the lessons of American "money doctors," transforming what was a means to build a colonial state on the cheap into a postcolonial moral imperative. Austerity became not just policy, but an ideology that transcended political divides and reshaped the boundaries of the Philippine economic imagination.
